en: Your elder Bakay said this,
Struck his gray steed once,
And called out, ‘Azhybay!’
He turned the gray steed's head.
Your elder, wolf-maned Bakay,
Shouting ‘Azhybay!’
Stood before him.
Argyn Khan's Azhybay
Awoke and rose from sleep,
Turning to his right,
Running in haste,
Gathering himself like a lion,
With his arms folded before Bakay,
He now gave a ringing greeting.
Turning his steed's head,
Your elder, hawk-like Bakay,
Returned his greeting.
Hero Azhybay said this,
Spoke wonders no man knew:
‘If you are Muslims, you two lions,
With blessings, peace be upon you!
Take me with you as a companion.
If you are unbelievers, you two lions,
Slaughter me as a sacrifice.
Kartküröng, the horse I ride,
Take him away as your booty.
Caught by surprise,
I stand here troubled.
I have no means to fight;
What can I do?
If I mount my horse and take a spear,
If I gird a sword at my side,
I too would be a hero like you.
I would say, “Where is calamity?”
I would devour whoever I encountered.
When I dwelt in my own land,
To Manas, son of Jakyp,
I wished to be a champion.
Long I lived in Chambyl.
With Bakay, the rich man's son,
From the first day my desire
Was to become a friend.
Unable to find those two,
With my uncommon valor,
I am one of the foremost heroes.
Yearning for those two heroes,
Renouncing my people,
I am one of the heroes brought to ruin.
Chasing wild asses on the barren plain,
I am one of the heroes who departed.
Girding a naked sword,
Going around the face of the earth,
The ear hears, but the eye does not see.
When shall I reach Talas?
To be a friend for the hereafter,
When shall I reach Manas?
I am one of those who set forth.
Khan Bakay appeared in my dream;
My own people, out on the plain,
I am one of those who left them behind.
I have no equal, I have no khan;
All the heroes are absent.
Places heard by the ear and seen by the eye,
How many lands I have roamed!
Such is this mischievous world!
Going about saying ‘Bakay, Manas,’
Of iron rope, a glaring red
Net is what I have fallen into.
My horse is thin, I myself am on foot;
I have fallen captive.
If you wish, leave me alive.
If you desire the Brown horse,
Slaughter me here on this spot.
Who would find a way for me,
Who would raise many battle cries,
Who would wrest me free,
Generous Manas is not here either.
Seen today, gone tomorrow,
When the dear soul is hard pressed,
Such is this mischievous world.
My wings wearied, following tracks,
I was a hero who came prepared.
Generous Bakay and Manas,
I was a hero who came seeking them.
Seeking a ridge whose pass stood high,
Seeking a hero greater than mortals,
Maddened with longing,
On the barren plain I met you,
Warriors, and fell captive to you.
When I dwelt in my own land,
I, Azhybay, was an outstanding champion.
Caught while seeking heroes,
Today I myself
Am a hare caught in a trap.
Today, unable to reach my comrades,
I stand here in ruin.
I have traversed the earthly world.
For Manas and Bakay,
This year I yearn exceedingly.
I was a wondrous steed; my mane-fat gone,
Now I have grown lean.
Unable to find the noble hawks,
Now I have become a wretch.
When I dwelt in Chambyl,
I sliced and ate horse-rump meat.
Leopard Manas and mighty Bakay,
If I went and joined those two,
I said I would lay Kangay waste.
The red spear and Zulpukor,
I said I would wield them.
If I met the valiant ones,
Against the whole world's people, I myself,
I said I would press into battle.
I have no shelter, no support,
I have no equal beside me,
The two heroes I seek are absent.’
Relating his sorrow then,
Azhybay spoke.
When they heard Azhybay's words,
The two khans then from their horses
Dismounted in their grandeur.
Hero Azhybay ran
And took both their horses.
Taking their lead ropes, tethering them,
With uncommon agility,
He tied them swiftly, in a trice.
Turning back, he ran
And came to Khan Manas.
His coat of mail flashing,
Calling like a young hawk,
Warrior Bakay then
Spoke words of a different kind:
‘Oh, my child, who wore his horse down to the ribs,
Across the whole face of the earth,
Who wandered in hardship,
Though I have not seen you or known you,
Argyn Khan's son,
Is noble Azhybay well?
My child, what you sought has been found;
Your traveler has met you on the road.
We too, unable to find you,
Have suffered hardship, dear brave one.
The leopard's guiding sign,
The bloodthirsty lion's companion.
Azhybay and Bakay, two khans,
Those are the names of us two.
We have golden thrones to mount;
Our good fortune has opened.
If we spoke until dawn,
Our words would never end.
Born while dwelling in Altay,
When he reached twelve,
He attacked the realm with a royal court,
Destroyed its palace and took booty.
There is your lion Manas!
Named Manas, the lion hero,
He received a letter from the unseen.
Named the bloodthirsty Burut,
In seething Beijing's
Register he was entered.’
Argyn Khan's Azhybay,
About bloodthirsty lion Manas,
From your wise elder Bakay,
He heard everything fully.
Between the two of them,
He became the bond that joined them.
When they heard Bakay's words,
Like the stars in the sky,
The three destroyers stirred.
For the other world then,
The three destroyers became friends.
Clasping hands, greeting one another,
Embracing and kissing,
Twelve limbs and forty veins,
Every one of them stirred.
Heroes bound until Judgment Day,
Embracing and becoming friends,
Like the mist upon the hills,
They grew pale together.
Meeting in the open wilds,
They had become friends.
Like the white antelope's hairs,
They became friends of one heart.
Like flour of white wheat,
They were kneaded into one.
Embracing and becoming friends,
Like a spring upon the hillside,
They now flowed freely together.
Of the wild-ass mares that had remained barren,
They slaughtered four or five at a time.
What would not fit in the traveling pot,
They skewered to roast.
Such was their giant nature:
They were still but half-fed.
Clasping hands,
The wolf-maned ones, bustling with joy,
Made their pledge.
Holding hands and speaking,
They declared their pledge firmly:
‘If we begin a holy war against unbelievers,
And one of us leaves another
Without giving him support,
May the oath sworn before God strike us!
May the sacred writing knotted in our belts strike us!
May Akkelte's bullet strike us!
May the blue matchcord's ember strike us!
Whoever turns back from wise counsel,
Whoever withdraws from the pledge,
May the shaggy-breasted earth strike him!
May the open-crowned sky strike him!
If Allah issues His decree,
If it falls upon our heads, let us face it.
If one of us happens to fall to a bullet,
Let us all die together!
Let us bundle our spears together,
Let us face the gunfire together,
Let us scout together,
Let us raise turmoil together.
Let our sheep share a fold,
Let us be companions at our meals;
Let us gather our gains together;
Let us share our faith when one dies.
Tamarisk-filled Keng-Kol, broad Talas,
Let us pasture in the choicest land.
Those who never shrink from combat,
Let us gather leopards and lions.
Let the horses grow fat and fit;
Let the gathered blue-maned ones number forty.
Let us dwell in the broad river valley;
Let us gather leaders never sated with blood.
Let us choose the skillful spearmen;
Let us gather the mighty who shake the world.
If we care for them and gather heroes,
If we gather all the peerless ones,
Drawing swords and sheathing them,
The brave-hearted warriors—
He was a hero born of saints—
Let Khan Bakay judge them.
Among the forty falcon heroes,
At the cry of ‘Enemy!’ losing heart,
Let there be no cowards.
Unable to catch and mount a horse,
Floundering, rushing, shouting,
Let there be no bunglers.
If a terrible, wretched enemy rises,
Beginning to flee and causing panic,
Let there be none who start that.
The vast people, suddenly,
Fleeing then and leaving them—
Let there be none who abandon them.
When charging, let them spare no enemy;
Among the forty falcon heroes,
Ruiners of the people, utterly vile,
Let there be no ignorant fools!”
Chewing white-wheat bread,
The champions in the open steppe
